# Speech and Audio Language Models {#sec-slm}

Two lines of development run through the preceding chapters. One is about
*understanding*: encoders trained by self-supervision (@sec-ssl) or weak
supervision (@sec-whisper) that turn audio into representations a downstream head
can read. The other is about *generation*: codecs (@sec-codecs) that turn audio
into tokens a language model can predict. This chapter is where they meet.

A **speech language model** — or, when the scope includes music and environmental
sound, an **audio language model** — is a system in which a large language model
consumes audio directly rather than a transcript of it, and in the fully general
case emits audio directly too. The promise is straightforward. A transcript
discards who is speaking, how they feel, whether they are joking, whether a dog
is barking, and when they stopped talking. A model that hears the waveform need
not discard any of it.

The reality is that these models are, at time of writing, noticeably less
intelligent than the text LLMs they are built from. That gap is the organising
question of this chapter, and it is more interesting than any individual
architecture.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading order and scope

This chapter assumes @sec-ssl (encoders), @sec-codecs (tokenisers), and
@sec-codec-lm (codec language modelling for synthesis). It deliberately does not
re-derive AudioLM, VALL-E, or Moshi's streaming mechanisms, which are treated as
*synthesis* in @sec-audiolm, @sec-valle, and @sec-tts-streaming. Here they are
components in a general-purpose model. The survey by Arora et al.
[@arora2025slmsurvey] is the reference work for this material and is a better
catalogue than this chapter attempts to be.
:::


## Three Architectures {#sec-slm-arch}

Almost every system in this space is one of three things.

| | **Cascade** | **Adapter (audio-in)** | **Native (audio-in, audio-out)** |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Structure | ASR $\to$ text LLM $\to$ TTS | Audio encoder $\to$ projector $\to$ LLM | Audio tokens in the LLM vocabulary, both directions |
| Sees | Transcript only | Encoder features | Tokens (and often text in parallel) |
| Latency | Sum of three stages | One stage | One stage, streamable |
| Text ability | **Fully preserved** | Degrades | Degrades more |
| Paralinguistics | Lost at the ASR boundary | Available in principle | Available in principle |
| Debuggability | Excellent — inspect the transcript | Poor | Poor |
| Examples | Most deployed voice assistants; Unmute | SALMONN, Qwen-Audio, Audio Flamingo | Moshi, GLM-4-Voice, Qwen2.5-Omni |

: Three architectures for speech language models. {#tbl-slm-arch}

The cascade deserves more respect than it usually receives. It preserves the
text LLM exactly — no forgetting, no degraded reasoning, full tool use and
instruction following — and every component can be swapped, monitored, and
tested independently. Its weaknesses are real but specific: latency accumulates,
ASR errors propagate irreversibly, and everything not in the transcript is gone
by the time the LLM sees anything. For a large class of assistant tasks that
last weakness costs nothing, which is why cascades remain the default in
production.

The interesting claim of the other two rows is that the discarded information
matters. Testing that claim honestly is harder than it looks, and @sec-slm-eval
returns to it.


## The Adapter Recipe {#sec-adapter}

The dominant architecture for audio understanding is a three-part sandwich, and
it is worth writing down precisely because almost everything reduces to it.

Let $\mathbf{X}$ be audio, $f_\theta$ a pretrained audio encoder (@sec-whisper-encoder),
and $\mathcal{P}_\phi$ a learned **projector**. The audio is converted to a
sequence of vectors in the LLM's *embedding* space and prepended to the text
embeddings:

$$
\mathbf{H} = \mathcal{P}_\phi\big(f_\theta(\mathbf{X})\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d_{\text{LLM}}},
\qquad
p(\mathbf{y}) = \prod_{i} p_{\text{LLM}}\big(y_i \mid \mathbf{H}, \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{y}_{<i})\big)
$$ {#eq-adapter}

The LLM is unmodified. It receives what it takes to be $M$ ordinary token
embeddings and continues as usual. This is the same trick that made vision-language
models work, transplanted without alteration.

The projector's real job is **rate reduction**, and the arithmetic explains most
design choices. Whisper's encoder emits 50 vectors per second; a one-minute clip
is 3,000 positions, which would dominate any reasonable context. Projectors
therefore downsample aggressively — by stacking adjacent frames before a linear
map, by strided convolution, or by cross-attending a fixed number of learned
queries into each window (a **Q-Former**). Typical operating points land between
5 and 12 vectors per second, a factor of 4–10 reduction.

Three systems established the design space.

**SALMONN** [@tang2024salmonn] uses *two* encoders in parallel — Whisper for
speech and BEATs for general audio events — concatenated frame-by-frame and read
by a window-level Q-Former, with LoRA adaptation of the LLM. The dual encoder is
the point: a speech encoder trained on transcription is systematically poor at
non-speech audio, which is exactly the WavLM/HuBERT specialisation of
@sec-wavlm reappearing one level up. SALMONN also reported **task
over-fitting** — after instruction tuning, the model collapses toward the tasks
it was tuned on and loses the emergent cross-modal abilities it briefly had —
and proposed a lightweight activation-tuning stage to recover them. That failure
recurs throughout this chapter.

**Qwen-Audio** [@chu2023qwenaudio] attacked the same problem from the data side,
training one encoder across more than thirty tasks with a hierarchy of tags
identifying task, language, and annotation granularity, so that supervision from
heterogeneous datasets could be shared rather than interfering. Qwen2-Audio
[@chu2024qwen2audio] dropped the tag hierarchy for natural-language prompts, and
Qwen2.5-Omni [@xu2025qwen25omni] extended the same backbone to vision and to
speech output.

**LTU** [@gong2024ltu] made the case that the interesting capability is not
classification but *reasoning about* audio — answering open-ended questions about
what is happening and why — and built the instruction corpus to train it. Audio
Flamingo [@kong2024audioflamingo; @ghosh2025audioflamingo2] pursued in-context
learning and long-audio understanding in the same spirit.


## Training and Catastrophic Forgetting {#sec-slm-training}

Training proceeds in stages, and the recipe is stable across systems.

1. **Modality alignment.** Freeze the LLM, train the projector alone on
   large-scale ASR and audio-captioning data. The objective is simply to make
   @eq-adapter produce embeddings the LLM can read.
2. **Instruction tuning.** Unfreeze partially — typically LoRA on the LLM, and
   often the encoder's upper layers — and train on audio question-answering and
   multi-task instruction data.
3. **Speech output**, where applicable: train the generation path
   (@sec-codec-lm), usually with the understanding path frozen.
4. **Preference optimisation and duplex adaptation**, increasingly standard.

The central difficulty is stage 2. **Speech-centric training degrades the
model's text abilities**, and the degradation is severe enough to be the
principal reported obstacle. Speech-IFEval [@lu2025speechifeval] isolates it by
separating instruction-following from speech perception, and finds that most
speech-aware LLMs "struggle with even basic instructions, performing far worse
than text-based LLMs", and are unstable under paraphrases of the same prompt.
A model that hears well but can no longer follow a formatting instruction is not
obviously an improvement on a cascade.

Two mitigations are in current use. The first is architectural conservatism:
keep the LLM frozen and push all adaptation into the projector, which preserves
text ability at the cost of how much audio detail can reach the model —
Freeze-Omni [@wang2024freezeomni] takes this position explicitly. The second is
to fix the *data*. DeSTA2.5-Audio [@lu2025desta25] observes that forgetting is
largely caused by training targets written in a style the backbone LLM would
never produce, and has the backbone **generate its own training targets** from
audio metadata, so that fine-tuning reinforces rather than overwrites its native
distribution. Reported gains hold across Dynamic-SUPERB, MMAU, SAKURA,
Speech-IFEval, and VoiceBench simultaneously, which is the kind of broad result
that suggests a real mechanism rather than benchmark tuning.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The synthetic-data trap

Most audio instruction corpora are built by synthesising speech from text with a
TTS system. Such data has *no genuine paralinguistic variation* — no real
emotion, no real hesitation, no real room. A model trained on it can only learn
that audio is a lossy encoding of text, which is precisely the failure the whole
paradigm exists to avoid. This is a plausible mechanism behind
@sec-modality-gap, and it is self-inflicted.
:::


## Speaking: Interleaving, Streams, and Duplex {#sec-slm-duplex}

Models that emit audio face a decision about how text participates in
generation. Nearly all of them use text somehow, and *why* is the interesting
part.

**Text-scaffolded generation** is the near-universal pattern. Rather than
modelling audio tokens alone, the model predicts text and audio jointly, with
text leading:

$$
p(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{w}) = \prod_{t} p\big(w_t \mid \mathbf{w}_{<t}, \mathbf{a}_{<t}\big)\,
p\big(\mathbf{a}_t \mid \mathbf{w}_{\leq t}, \mathbf{a}_{<t}\big)
$$ {#eq-interleave}

Two families implement @eq-interleave differently. **Interleaving** alternates
chunks of text and audio tokens in one sequence — the approach of SpeechGPT
[@zhang2023speechgpt], AudioPaLM [@rubenstein2023audiopalm], and GLM-4-Voice
[@zeng2024glm4voice]. **Parallel streams** predict text and audio at the same
position on separate channels, which is Moshi's *inner monologue*
(@sec-tts-streaming). Mini-Omni [@xie2024miniomni] and LLaMA-Omni
[@fang2024llamaomni] occupy points in between, generating text and audio
concurrently to keep latency low.

The empirical finding is consistent and slightly deflating: **the text stream
carries most of the reasoning**. Moshi's ablations show the inner monologue
improves linguistic quality substantially. Volhejn's reading of this is that
most of the intelligence is delegated to text while the audio streams degenerate
into an integrated ASR and TTS — which, if true, means the architecture is a
cascade wearing a different coat. I think that is too strong as a general claim,
but it is the right worry, and no current system clearly refutes it.

**Full duplex** is the other axis. A half-duplex model processes one turn at a
time; a full-duplex model listens and speaks simultaneously, which is what makes
interruption, backchannelling ("mm-hm"), and overlap representable at all.
Modelling both participants' audio as parallel streams (@sec-tts-streaming)
replaces an explicit turn-taking state machine with next-token prediction, and
dGSLM [@nguyen2023dgslm] demonstrated the idea before speech LLMs existed by
modelling two-channel spontaneous dialogue directly. Full-Duplex-Bench
[@lin2025fullduplexbench] gives the behaviours their own metrics: pause
handling, backchannelling, turn-taking, and interruption management.


## The Modality Gap {#sec-modality-gap}

Here is the phenomenon, in the cleanest available form. Ask a natively
speech-capable model, in a high-pitched voice, *"Am I speaking in a low voice or
a high voice?"* It will generally fail — not by refusing, but by answering as
though it had read a transcript. Volhejn reports this for Gemini, ChatGPT's
Advanced Voice Mode, Qwen, and Moshi alike.

This is a strange failure. The information is unambiguously present in the input,
the model was trained on audio, and the question is trivial. Four mechanisms
plausibly contribute, and they are not mutually exclusive.

**Tokenisation discards it by construction.** Semantic tokens are *defined* by
invariance to speaker and channel — the demonstration in @sec-semantic-acoustic,
where fixing semantic tokens and resampling the rest yields the same words in a
different voice, shows this directly. A model whose loss is dominated by semantic
tokens is trained to ignore exactly the cues in question. The layer-wise result of
@sec-layerwise says the same thing about encoders: representations optimised for
content actively suppress paralinguistic nuisance variables.

**Text scaffolding makes audio vestigial.** If @eq-interleave lets the model
route all reasoning through text, gradient pressure on the audio path to encode
anything beyond phonetic content is weak.

**The training data has no variation to learn from.** The synthetic-data trap
above.

**Scale asymmetry.** Text corpora are trillions of tokens; transcribed and
instruction-annotated speech is orders of magnitude smaller, and the annotated
paralinguistic slice smaller still.

The measurements support a sharper diagnosis than "the model cannot hear". SAKURA
[@yang2025sakura] evaluates multi-hop reasoning over speech and audio and finds
that models fail to integrate audio information into a reasoning chain **even
when they extract the relevant information correctly**. Perception is not the
bottleneck; *integration* is. Consistently, a 2026 layer-wise study
[@yang2026paralinguistic] finds that paralinguistic and semantic information
occupy identifiable and distinct layers of these models, and that fine-tuning
*selected* layers with an auxiliary classification head restores paralinguistic
awareness more effectively than fine-tuning everything. The information is
present and localisable; the model is simply not in the habit of using it.

That is a more optimistic reading than the phenomenon first suggests. It says the
gap is a training and objective-design problem rather than a representational
impossibility.


## The Tasks That Became Prompts {#sec-slm-tasks}

A striking side-effect of this architecture is that a set of previously separate
research areas collapsed into prompting. Each once had its own models, losses,
and leaderboards; each is now a question you ask.

| Task | Classical formulation | Standard data | Now |
|:-----|:----------------------|:--------------|:----|
| **Spoken language understanding** | Intent classification + slot filling, or a cascade through ASR | SLURP [@bastianelli2020slurp] | "What does the user want?" |
| **Audio captioning** | Encoder-decoder trained on audio-text pairs | Clotho [@drossos2020clotho], AudioCaps | "Describe what you hear." |
| **Sound event classification** | Multi-label classification over an ontology | AudioSet [@gemmeke2017audioset] | "What sounds are present?" |
| **Speech emotion recognition** | Categorical or valence-arousal classification | IEMOCAP, MSP-Podcast | "How does the speaker feel?" |
| **Speech translation** | Cascade or end-to-end sequence model (@sec-st) | CoVoST 2, FLEURS | "Translate this into German." |

: Audio tasks absorbed into instruction prompting. {#tbl-slm-tasks}

Two caveats keep this from being the whole story. Specialised models still win on
their own tasks, often by a wide margin, and the unified model's advantage is
breadth and compositionality rather than peak accuracy; @sec-paralinguistics
takes these tasks on their own terms, including the measurement problems the
prompting framing inherits. And **contrastive
audio-text models** remain a distinct and more efficient paradigm for
retrieval-style problems: CLAP [@elizalde2023clap] aligns audio and text in a
shared embedding space, giving zero-shot classification over an open label set
at a fraction of the cost of generative inference.


## Evaluation {#sec-slm-eval}

Evaluating these models is harder than evaluating either parent, because the
output is open-ended text about an open-ended input.

| Benchmark | Measures |
|:----------|:---------|
| **Dynamic-SUPERB** [@huang2024dynamicsuperb] | Instruction-following across many held-out speech tasks; the SUPERB idea (@sec-superb) rebuilt for prompting |
| **AIR-Bench** [@yang2024airbench] | Generative comprehension over speech, sound, and music; foundation and chat splits |
| **AudioBench** [@wang2024audiobench] | Broad understanding suite spanning speech, sound, and paralinguistics |
| **MMAU** [@sakshi2025mmau] | Expert-level reasoning over speech, sound, and music |
| **SAKURA** [@yang2025sakura] | Multi-hop reasoning that requires integrating audio evidence |
| **VoiceBench** [@chen2024voicebench] | End-to-end voice-assistant quality under realistic speaker and noise variation |
| **Speech-IFEval** [@lu2025speechifeval] | Instruction-following and catastrophic forgetting, measured separately from perception |
| **Full-Duplex-Bench** [@lin2025fullduplexbench] | Turn-taking, backchannelling, pauses, interruptions |

: Benchmarks for speech and audio language models. {#tbl-slm-eval}

Three methodological problems are worth naming, because they affect how the
numbers in these tables should be read.

**Many questions are answerable from the transcript alone.** If a benchmark item
can be solved by an ASR-plus-text-LLM cascade, it measures nothing about audio
understanding. The correct control is to *run that cascade* and report it as a
baseline — a practice that is becoming standard but is still often omitted. Any
claim that native audio processing helps should be a claim about the gap to that
baseline.

**Open-ended answers are usually scored by an LLM judge**, which inherits the
judge's biases, is sensitive to answer formatting, and has received little
meta-evaluation in this domain. This is the same problem flagged for synthesis in
@sec-tts-eval, and it is not better here.

**Perception and instruction-following are routinely conflated.** A model can
fail an item because it did not hear correctly or because it ignored the output
format. Speech-IFEval exists precisely to separate the two, and the finding that
much of the apparent perception failure is really instruction failure should make
one cautious about single-number leaderboards.


## Open Problems {#sec-slm-open}

1. **Closing the modality gap.** The evidence in @sec-modality-gap suggests
   paralinguistic information is present but unused. Whether the fix is
   objective design, better data, selective adaptation, or richer tokenisation is
   the field's central open question.
2. **Forgetting without a trade-off.** Every current method buys text ability
   with audio detail or vice versa. A training scheme that adds hearing without
   subtracting reasoning does not yet exist.
3. **Beating the cascade convincingly.** On most benchmarks a strong cascade
   remains competitive. Establishing where native processing genuinely wins —
   and by how much — is unresolved, and partly an evaluation problem.
4. **Long-form audio.** Rate reduction in @eq-adapter makes minutes tractable
   and hours not. Meetings, lectures, and podcasts remain out of reach without
   chunking that destroys global structure.
5. **Duplex behaviour is barely modelled.** Knowing when to speak, when to stay
   silent, and when to yield is a skill with almost no supervision available,
   and Full-Duplex-Bench shows current systems handle it crudely.
6. **Speaker attribution in multi-party audio.** These models largely assume one
   speaker. Integrating diarization (@sec-speaker-diarization) into a speech LLM, rather
   than bolting it on, is open.
7. **Safety at the paralinguistic layer.** A model that can hear emotion, health
   markers, age, and identity can also infer them without consent, and a model
   that can speak in any voice can impersonate. Neither the inference side nor
   the generation side has an accepted governance story.
8. **Scaling laws.** Nobody has mapped how audio-language capability trades off
   between audio hours, text tokens, parameters, and token rate.


## Summary

Speech and audio language models are the convergence point of this part of the
book: the encoders of @sec-ssl supply perception, the codecs of @sec-codecs
supply a generation interface, and a pretrained text LLM supplies everything
else. Three architectures divide the space — the cascade, which preserves text
ability perfectly and discards everything not in the transcript; the adapter
sandwich of @eq-adapter, which projects encoder features into the LLM's embedding
space and is essentially the vision-language recipe unchanged; and native
token-in-token-out models that read and write audio directly.

The recurring technical difficulty is that teaching a language model to hear
tends to make it worse at thinking. Instruction tuning on audio degrades text
ability measurably, task-specific tuning collapses emergent generality, and the
mitigations — frozen backbones, selective adaptation, self-generated training
targets — all trade one capability against another.

The recurring *scientific* difficulty is the modality gap. A model that hears a
high-pitched voice and cannot say so is failing at something its input contains
and its architecture permits. The most useful recent finding is that this is not
a perception failure: the information is extractable, and localisable to
particular layers, but does not make it into the model's reasoning. Tokenisers
that define away paralinguistics, text scaffolding that renders the audio path
vestigial, and synthetic training data with no genuine acoustic variation all
push in the same direction. That the causes are identifiable and largely
self-inflicted is the best reason to expect the gap to close.
